standard.title: Tone, intonation and stress to express feelings and opinions
standard.description: use tone-syllables, intonation, stress and phrasing to express feelings and opinions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can produce tones with developing accuracy and explain the phonetic system as a learning tool (AC9LCH4U01). They can recite texts with attention to tone and rhythm. They have not yet deliberately used tonal variation, intonation and stress to convey emotional register and opinion, or used digital tools to monitor and develop spoken fluency.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use tone-syllables, intonation, stress and phrasing deliberately to express feelings, opinions and emotional register in spoken target language, with developing fluency.

nodes.label: Intonation and stress for emotional register
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can deliberately vary intonation, stress and phrasing to convey different emotional registers — happiness, sadness, concern, emphasis — in the target language.
nodes.minimum_width: Read or say the same sentence with at least two different emotional registers, demonstrating how intonation and stress change to convey each.
nodes.typical_width: Use intonation, stress and phrasing to express different emotions and registers; read lyrics, poems, news and familiar texts aloud with attention to tonal and intonation patterns; explore how the same words with different intonation convey different meanings; play speaking games demonstrating different emotions.
wider: Investigate how intonation patterns in statements, questions and exclamations differ in the target language from English — identify where the patterns are similar and where they diverge
Compare how the same emotional register (e.g. urgency, enthusiasm, concern) is conveyed through intonation differently across the target language and English
nodes.hinge_reason: Deliberate use of intonation and stress is the prerequisite for expressive spoken production. Students who produce target language at a flat, uniform pitch cannot convey emotional register or opinion in speech — which undermines the authenticity and communicative effectiveness of all spoken interaction.

response_modes.reason: Intonation and stress control requires repeated oral production practice with feedback. Regular reading aloud, performance tasks and self-recording activities build the expressive fluency that deliberate intonation control requires.

success_criteria: Reads or speaks the same sentence with at least two different emotional registers, demonstrating distinguishable intonation or stress changes
Can identify and explain what tonal or intonation feature creates the different emotional effect

nodes.label: Tone change patterns and phrasing
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and apply tone change patterns in the target language and use phrasing — pausing, grouping, rhythm — to support fluent and expressive spoken production.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one tone change pattern in the target language (e.g. where a standard tone changes in a specific phonological context) and demonstrate correct application in at least three examples.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise and apply tone change patterns; use phrasing — grouping words, pausing at appropriate points — to support fluency and intelligibility; understand how tone marks affect pronunciation and meaning; use context to distinguish between homophones or tonal minimal pairs.
wider: Analyse a spoken text for phrasing patterns — identify where the speaker pauses, groups words, and varies stress, and explain how these choices support comprehension
Investigate tone sandhi or tone change rules in the target language — compile examples and explain the phonological context for each change

response_modes.reason: Tone change patterns require explicit instruction — they are not intuitive and background learners who know spoken language may not have analysed these patterns. Systematic explanation of phonological contexts for tone change, followed by targeted practice, prevents persistent errors.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Background learners often apply tone change patterns correctly in speech without being able to articulate the rule. Width investment here bridges the gap between implicit oral knowledge and explicit metalinguistic understanding — building the analytical capacity to teach and explain the language to others.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one tone change pattern and demonstrates correct application in at least three examples
Uses phrasing and grouping to support comprehension in at least one spoken text

nodes.label: Using digital tools for fluency development
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use digital tools — recording apps, pronunciation checkers, digital texts — to monitor and develop their own spoken fluency.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a digital tool to record and review at least one spoken production, identifying at least one specific feature to improve and practising improvement.
nodes.typical_width: Use digital tools to check pronunciation and tonal accuracy; record own speech and compare with models; use voice-recording apps and online resources to develop fluency; check pronunciation of target language words using digital dictionaries or reference tools.
wider: Conduct a systematic self-review of a recorded spoken performance — identify specific tonal, intonation or fluency targets, practise, re-record, and compare the two versions
Use digital tools to investigate regional accent variation in the target language — compare recordings from different communities and identify phonological differences

response_modes.reason: Digital tool use for fluency development integrates intonation awareness (node 1) and tone change knowledge (node 2) into a self-directed improvement cycle. The teaching investment is in establishing a sustainable self-review practice — not a one-off recording task but a regular cycle of production, review and improvement.

success_criteria: Uses a digital tool to record and review at least one spoken production
Identifies at least one specific fluency target from the review and demonstrates a practice attempt
